claim: GE23077 (GE) is a cyclic-peptide antibiotic produced by the soil bacterium Actinomadura sp. DSMZ 13491.
source: GE23077 (GE) is a cyclic-peptide antibiotic produced by the soil bacterium Actinomadura sp. DSMZ 13491 (Figure 1A; Ciciliato et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ciciliato et al., 2004

claim: GE exhibits antibacterial activity against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacterial pathogens in culture, including Moraxella catarrhalis and Streptococcus pyogenes.
source: GE exhibits antibacterial activity against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacterial pathogens in culture, including Moraxella catarrhalis and Streptococcus pyogenes (Supplementary file 1A; Ciciliato et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1A and citation to Ciciliato et al., 2004

claim: GE inhibits both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) in vitro.
source: GE inhibits both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) in vitro, but does not inhibit human RNAP I, II, or III in vitro (Supplementary file 1B; Ciciliato et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1B and citation to Ciciliato et al., 2004

claim: GE does not inhibit human RNAP I, II, or III in vitro.
source: GE inhibits both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) in vitro, but does not inhibit human RNAP I, II, or III in vitro (Supplementary file 1B; Ciciliato et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1B and citation to Ciciliato et al., 2004

claim: Analysis of the kinetics of inhibition suggests that GE inhibits RNAP at a stage subsequent to the formation of the RNAP-template complex.
source: Analysis of the kinetics of inhibition suggests that GE inhibits RNAP at a stage subsequent to the formation of the RNAP-template complex (Sarubbi et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sarubbi et al., 2004

claim: GE is a non-ribosomally-synthesized cyclic heptapeptide.
source: GE is a non-ribosomally-synthesized cyclic heptapeptide (Figure 1A; Marazzi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marazzi et al., 2005

claim: The stereochemistry at four chiral centers of GE has been defined based on acid hydrolysis and gas chromatography.
source: The stereochemistry at four chiral centers of GE has been defined based on acid hydrolysis and gas chromatography, but the stereochemistry at five other chiral centers has not been defined (Figure 1A; Marazzi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marazzi et al., 2005

claim: The stereochemistry at five chiral centers of GE has not been defined.
source: The stereochemistry at four chiral centers of GE has been defined based on acid hydrolysis and gas chromatography, but the stereochemistry at five other chiral centers has not been defined (Figure 1A; Marazzi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marazzi et al., 2005

claim: Analogs of GE having modifications of the dmaDap, dhGln, and Ama residues have been prepared by semi-synthetic derivatization of GE.
source: Analogs of GE having modifications of the dmaDap, dhGln, and Ama residues, have been prepared by semi-synthetic derivatization of GE (Mariani et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mariani et al., 2005

claim: GE does not inhibit formation of a competitor-resistant RNAP-promoter open complex (RPo).
source: Figure 1B shows that GE does not inhibit steps in transcription initiation up to and including formation of a competitor-resistant RNAP-promoter open complex (RPo).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: GE does not inhibit promoter binding, loading of promoter DNA into the RNAP active-center cleft, or promoter unwinding.
source: We infer that GE does not inhibit promoter binding, loading of promoter DNA into the RNAP active-center cleft, or promoter unwinding.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GE does not inhibit RPo formation

claim: GE inhibits nucleotide addition in transcription initiation.
source: The results in Figure 1C show that GE inhibits nucleotide addition in transcription initiation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: GE inhibits both primer-dependent transcription initiation and de novo transcription initiation.
source: GE inhibits both primer-dependent transcription initiation (Figure 1C), and de novo transcription initiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: In primer-dependent transcription initiation, GE inhibits the first nucleotide-addition step, inhibiting the synthesis of a 3-nt RNA product from a 2-nt RNA primer and an NTP.
source: In primer-dependent transcription initiation, GE inhibits the first nucleotide-addition step, inhibiting the synthesis of a 3-nt RNA product from a 2-nt RNA primer and an NTP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text

claim: In de novo transcription initiation, GE inhibits the first nucleotide-addition step, inhibiting the synthesis of a 2-nt RNA product from initiating NTPs.
source: In de novo transcription initiation, GE inhibits the first nucleotide-addition step, inhibiting the synthesis of a 2-nt RNA product from initiating NTPs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text

claim: GE does not inhibit nucleotide addition in transcription elongation.
source: The results in Figure 1D show that GE does not inhibit nucleotide addition in transcription elongation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: GE does not inhibit transcription elongation upon addition of NTPs to a halted elongation complex.
source: GE does not inhibit transcription elongation upon addition of NTPs to a halted elongation complex (Figure 1D), and GE does not inhibit single nucleotide addition upon addition of an NTP to an elongation complex reconstituted from RNAP and a synthetic nucleic acid scaffold (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: GE does not inhibit single nucleotide addition upon addition of an NTP to an elongation complex reconstituted from RNAP and a synthetic nucleic acid scaffold.
source: GE does not inhibit transcription elongation upon addition of NTPs to a halted elongation complex (Figure 1D), and GE does not inhibit single nucleotide addition upon addition of an NTP to an elongation complex reconstituted from RNAP and a synthetic nucleic acid scaffold (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: GE specifically inhibits nucleotide addition in transcription initiation.
source: We conclude that GE specifically inhibits nucleotide addition in transcription initiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GE inhibits nucleotide addition in initiation but not in elongation

claim: GE functions through a binding site that is available in RPo but that is not available in an elongation complex.
source: The observation that GE inhibits nucleotide addition in initiation but not in elongation suggests that GE functions through a binding site that is available in RPo but that is not available in an elongation complex—for example, a binding site that overlaps the RNAP active-center i and i+1 nucleotide binding sites, or the path of the RNA product from the i and i+1 nucleotide binding sites, and that therefore would be unoccupied in RPo but occupied by RNA in an elongation complex.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of GE on initiation versus elongation

claim: Rifampin (Rif) does not inhibit formation of RPo.
source: Like GE, Rif does not inhibit formation of RPo (Figure 1B; McClure and Cech, 1978).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1B and citation to McClure and Cech, 1978

claim: Rif inhibits nucleotide addition in transcription initiation, but does not inhibit nucleotide addition in transcription elongation.
source: Also like GE, Rif inhibits nucleotide addition in transcription initiation, but does not inhibit nucleotide addition in transcription elongation (Figure 1C,D; Sippel and Hartmann, 1968).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1C,D and citation to Sippel and Hartmann, 1968

claim: Rif does not generally inhibit the first nucleotide-addition step in transcription initiation.
source: However, in contrast to GE, Rif does not generally inhibit the first nucleotide-addition step in transcription initiation (Figure 1C; McClure and Cech, 1978).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1C and citation to McClure and Cech, 1978

claim: Rif generally only inhibits synthesis of >2–3-nt RNA products by binding to a site along the path of RNA from the RNAP active-center and sterically blocking RNA extension.
source: Rif generally only inhibits synthesis of >2–3-nt RNA products and does so by binding to a site along the path of RNA from the RNAP active-center and sterically blocking RNA extension (Campbell et al., 2001; Feklistov et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Campbell et al., 2001 and Feklistov et al., 2008

claim: GE inhibits synthesis of 2-nt RNA products, whereas Rif generally only inhibits synthesis of >2–3-nt RNA products.
source: The observation that GE inhibits synthesis of 2-nt RNA products, whereas Rif generally only inhibits synthesis of >2–3-nt RNA products, suggests that GE functions through a binding site located closer than the Rif binding site to the RNAP active-center.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of GE and Rif inhibition patterns

claim: GE functions through a binding site located closer than the Rif binding site to the RNAP active-center.
source: The observation that GE inhibits synthesis of 2-nt RNA products, whereas Rif generally only inhibits synthesis of >2–3-nt RNA products, suggests that GE functions through a binding site located closer than the Rif binding site to the RNAP active-center.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of GE and Rif inhibition patterns

claim: Sorangicin (Sor) functions through the same binding site on RNAP as Rif and inhibits synthesis only of >2–3-nt RNA products.
source: Sorangicin (Sor) functions through the same binding site on RNAP as Rif and inhibits synthesis only of >2–3-nt RNA products (Campbell et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campbell et al., 2005

claim: Myxopyronin (Myx), corallopyronin (Cor), ripostatin (Rip), and lipiarmycin (Lpm) inhibit formation of RPo.
source: Myxopyronin (Myx), corallopyronin (Cor), ripostatin (Rip), and lipiarmycin (Lpm) inhibit formation of RPo (Ho et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ho et al., 2009

claim: Streptolydigin (Stl), CBR703 (CBR), and microcin J25 (MccJ25) inhibit nucleotide addition in both initiation and elongation.
source: Streptolydigin (Stl), CBR703 (CBR), and microcin J25 (MccJ25) inhibit nucleotide addition in both initiation and elongation (Artsimovitch et al., 2003; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2004; Ho et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Artsimovitch et al., 2003, Mukhopadhyay et al., 2004, and Ho et al., 2009

claim: GE inhibits transcription through a novel mechanism.
source: We conclude that GE inhibits transcription through a novel mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with other RNAP inhibitors

claim: 33 independent single-substitution GER mutants were identified through saturation mutagenesis of genes encoding Escherichia coli RNAP β and β′ subunits.
source: We identified 33 independent single-substitution GER mutants (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: All GER mutants mapped to the RNAP β subunit.
source: All mapped to the RNAP β subunit (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The GER substitutions comprised six distinct substitutions at three sites in RNAP β: residues 565, 566, and 684.
source: The GER substitutions comprised six distinct substitutions at three sites in RNAP β: residues 565, 566, and 684 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: All six GER substitutions result in at least moderate resistance (≥fourfold higher MIC).
source: Minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) assays indicate that all six GER substitutions result in at least moderate resistance (≥fourfold higher MIC) and that two result in high-level resistance (≥16-fold higher MIC; Figure 2A; Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2B

claim: Two GER substitutions result in high-level resistance (≥16-fold higher MIC).
source: Minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) assays indicate that all six GER substitutions result in at least moderate resistance (≥fourfold higher MIC) and that two result in high-level resistance (≥16-fold higher MIC; Figure 2A; Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2B

claim: Each GER mutant is able to complement an rpoBts mutant for growth at the non-permissive temperature, indicating that each GER RNAP derivative is sufficiently functional in transcription to support viability.
source: Complementation assays indicate that each GER mutant is able to complement an rpoBts mutant for growth at the non-permissive temperature, indicating that each GER RNAP derivative is sufficiently functional in transcription to support viability (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: RNAP purified from GER mutants exhibited resistance in vitro.
source: RNAP purified from GER mutants exhibited resistance in vitro (Figure 2B), indicating that the GER phenotype at the cellular level is attributable to resistance at the enzymatic level.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The GER phenotype at the cellular level is attributable to resistance at the enzymatic level.
source: RNAP purified from GER mutants exhibited resistance in vitro (Figure 2B), indicating that the GER phenotype at the cellular level is attributable to resistance at the enzymatic level.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that purified RNAP from GER mutants exhibits resistance

claim: RNAP is the functional cellular target for GE.
source: We conclude that RNAP is the functional cellular target for GE, and that RNAP β residues 565, 566, and 684 comprise a determinant essential for transcription inhibition by GE.
evidence: Inferred from genetic and biochemical data

claim: RNAP β residues 565, 566, and 684 comprise a determinant essential for transcription inhibition by GE.
source: We conclude that RNAP is the functional cellular target for GE, and that RNAP β residues 565, 566, and 684 comprise a determinant essential for transcription inhibition by GE.
evidence: Inferred from genetic and biochemical data

claim: The sites of GER substitutions are located adjacent to each other and form a compact determinant ('GE target').
source: In the three-dimensional structure of RNAP, the sites of GER substitutions are located adjacent to each other and form a compact determinant ('GE target'; Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: The GE target is located in the RNAP active-center region.
source: The GE target is located in the RNAP active-center region (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: The GE target overlaps the RNAP active-center i and i+1 nucleotide binding sites.
source: The GE target overlaps the RNAP active-center i and i+1 nucleotide binding sites, and comprises residues in two active-center subregions: the 'D2 loop' and the 'link region' (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The GE target comprises residues in two active-center subregions: the 'D2 loop' and the 'link region'.
source: The GE target overlaps the RNAP active-center i and i+1 nucleotide binding sites, and comprises residues in two active-center subregions: the 'D2 loop' and the 'link region' (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The RNAP active center contains two nucleotide binding sites—the i site and the i+1 site--flanking the catalytic Mg2+ ion, Mg2+(I).
source: The RNAP active center contains two nucleotide binding sites—the i site and the i+1 site--flanking the catalytic Mg2+ ion, Mg2+(I) (Zhang and Landick, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang and Landick, 2009

claim: The i site serves as the binding site for the first initiating NTP in de novo transcription initiation, and as the binding site for the 3′-nucleotide of the RNA primer in primer-dependent transcription initiation and RNA product in transcription elongation.
source: The i site serves as the binding site for the first initiating NTP in de novo transcription initiation, and as the binding site for the 3′-nucleotide of the RNA primer in primer-dependent transcription initiation and RNA product in transcription elongation.
evidence: Established knowledge about RNAP active center

claim: The i+1 site serves as the binding site for the second initiating NTP in de novo transcription initiation, and as the binding site for the extending NTP in primer-dependent transcription initiation and transcription elongation.
source: The i+1 site serves as the binding site for the second initiating NTP in de novo transcription initiation, and as the binding site for the extending NTP in primer-dependent transcription initiation and transcription elongation (Zhang and Landick, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang and Landick, 2009

claim: The D2 loop and the link region play roles in nucleotide addition, transcriptional fidelity, and transcriptional pausing.
source: The D2 loop and the link region play roles in nucleotide addition, transcriptional fidelity, and transcriptional pausing (Libby et al., 1989; Landick et al., 1990; Toulokhonov et al., 2007; Weinzierl 2010, 2012; Gordon et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: GE inhibits RNAP through direct interference with the function of the i and i+1 nucleotide binding sites and/or of Mg2+(I).
source: The location of the GE target suggests that GE inhibits RNAP through direct interference with the function of the i and i+1 nucleotide binding sites and/or of Mg2+(I).
evidence: Inferred from the location of the GE target

claim: The GE target is located approximately midway between Mg2+(I) and the Rif target.
source: The GE target is located approximately midway between Mg2+(I) and the Rif target (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2C,D

claim: The GE target is located adjacent to, but does not overlap, the Rif target.
source: The GE target is located adjacent to, but does not overlap, the Rif target (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: GER mutants do not exhibit cross-resistance with Rif.
source: Consistent with the absence of overlap, GER mutants do not exhibit cross-resistance with Rif (Figure 2E; Supplementary file 2D), and, conversely, RifR mutants do not exhibit cross-resistance with GE (Figure 2F; Supplementary file 2E; Ciciliato et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Supplementary file 2D

claim: RifR mutants do not exhibit cross-resistance with GE.
source: Consistent with the absence of overlap, GER mutants do not exhibit cross-resistance with Rif (Figure 2E; Supplementary file 2D), and, conversely, RifR mutants do not exhibit cross-resistance with GE (Figure 2F; Supplementary file 2E; Ciciliato et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F, Supplementary file 2E, and citation to Ciciliato et al., 2004

claim: The GE target does not overlap the targets of the previously characterized RNAP inhibitors Sor, Myx, Cor, Rip, Lpm, Stl, and CBR703.
source: The GE target also does not overlap the targets of the previously characterized RNAP inhibitors Sor, Myx, Cor, Rip, Lpm, Stl, and CBR703 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: GER mutants exhibit no cross-resistance with Sor, Myx, Cor, Rip, Lpm, Stl, and CBR703.
source: Accordingly, GER mutants exhibit no cross-resistance with Sor, Myx, Cor, Rip, Lpm, Stl, and CBR703 (Supplementary file 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Supplementary file 2F

claim: The GE target is strikingly small.
source: The GE target is strikingly small.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with other RNAP inhibitor targets

claim: The GE target comprises only six substitutions and only three sites in E. coli RNAP.
source: The GE target comprises only six substitutions and only three sites in E. coli RNAP (Figure 2A), and has dimensions of just ∼16 Å × ∼10 Å × ∼9 Å (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and structural analysis in Figure 2C

claim: The GE target has dimensions of just ∼16 Å × ∼10 Å × ∼9 Å.
source: The GE target comprises only six substitutions and only three sites in E. coli RNAP (Figure 2A), and has dimensions of just ∼16 Å × ∼10 Å × ∼9 Å (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: The GE target is much smaller than the Rif target (71 substitutions and 27 sites; ∼30 Å × ∼25 Å × ∼10 Å).
source: The GE target is much smaller than the Rif target (71 substitutions and 27 sites; ∼30 Å × ∼25 Å × ∼10 Å; Figure 2D; Jin and Gross, 1988; Severinov et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by comparison with data from Jin and Gross, 1988 and Severinov et al., 1993

claim: The genetically defined GE target corresponds to just part of the GE binding site on RNAP, not the full GE binding site on RNAP.
source: We infer that the genetically defined GE target corresponds to just part of the GE binding site on RNAP, not the full GE binding site on RNAP (in contrast to the genetically defined targets of Rif and other previously characterized RNAP inhibitors, which correspond to full inhibitor binding sites; Ho et al., 2009).
evidence: Inferred from the small size of the GE target relative to GE

claim: The full GE binding site on RNAP includes not only the genetically-defined GE target, but also evolutionarily invariant, functionally essential, residues of the RNAP active center that cannot be substituted without loss of RNAP function.
source: Specifically, we infer that the GE binding site comprises not only the residues at which GER substitutions are obtained, but also evolutionarily invariant, functionally essential, residues of the RNAP active center that cannot be substituted without loss of RNAP function, and thus cannot be substituted to confer GE-resistance.
evidence: Inferred from the small size of the GE target and the location of the target

claim: The frequency of spontaneous mutations yielding target-dependent GE-resistance is expected to be unusually small (∼1/10 to ∼1/5 the frequency of spontaneous mutations yielding target-dependent resistance to Rif and other RNAP inhibitors).
source: Namely, the frequency of spontaneous mutations yielding target-dependent GE-resistance is expected to be unusually small (∼1/10 to ∼1/5 the frequency of spontaneous mutations yielding target-dependent resistance to Rif and other RNAP inhibitors).
evidence: Inferred from the small size of the GE target-based resistance spectrum

claim: GE binds to the genetically-defined GE target.
source: Figure 3A shows that GE binds to the genetically-defined GE target, confirming the hypothesis that the GE target represents a determinant for binding of GE to RNAP.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3A

claim: GE occupies the RNAP i and i+1 sites and makes direct interactions with the D2 loop, the link region, and an RNAP Asp residue and water molecule that coordinate Mg2+(I).
source: The structure shows that GE occupies the RNAP i and i+1 sites and makes direct interactions with the D2 loop, the link region, and an RNAP Asp residue and water molecule that coordinate Mg2+(I) (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3B–E

claim: GE inhibits RNAP by directly interfering with function of the i and i+1 sites and/or Mg2+(I).
source: The structure provides strong support to the hypothesis that GE inhibits RNAP by directly interfering with function of the i and i+1 sites and/or Mg2+(I).
evidence: Inferred from crystal structure data

claim: All residues at which GER substitutions were obtained make direct contact with GE in the crystal structure: βGlu565, βGly566, βMet681, and βAsn684.
source: All residues at which GER substitutions were obtained make direct contact with GE in the crystal structure: βGlu565, βGly566, βMet681, and βAsn684 (green in Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The sidechain of βGlu565 penetrates the GE macrocycle and makes interactions with six of seven GE residues.
source: The sidechain of βGlu565 penetrates the GE macrocycle and makes interactions with six of seven GE residues (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3C–E

claim: Besides the residues at which GER substitutions were obtained, 11 additional residues—all located in the RNAP active-center i and i+1 sites—make direct interactions with GE in the crystal structure.
source: Besides the residues at which GER substitutions were obtained, 11 additional residues—all located in the RNAP active-center i and i+1 sites—make direct interactions with GE in the crystal structure: βPro564, βAsn568, βArg678, βMet685, βGln688, βLys1065, βLys1073, βHis1237, β′Asp462, β'Thr786, and β'Ala787 (cyan in Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3C

claim: 10 of the 11 additional residues that contact GE are invariant in RNAP from bacteria to humans.
source: 10 of these additional residues are invariant in RNAP from bacteria to humans (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and, for six, it is known that substitutions result in a loss of RNAP function (Kashlev et al., 1990; Mustaev et al., 1991; Sagitov et al., 1993; Sosunov et al., 2005; Jovanovic et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations

claim: For six of the additional residues that contact GE, it is known that substitutions result in a loss of RNAP function.
source: 10 of these additional residues are invariant in RNAP from bacteria to humans (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and, for six, it is known that substitutions result in a loss of RNAP function (Kashlev et al., 1990; Mustaev et al., 1991; Sagitov et al., 1993; Sosunov et al., 2005; Jovanovic et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The experimental electron density and inferred bonding patterns in the crystal structure define the stereochemistry at the five previously unassigned stereocenters of GE, as follows: D-dmaDap, D-Ser, D-Val, 3R,4S,L-dhGln, D-aThr, D-iSer, and L-Ama.
source: The experimental electron density and inferred bonding patterns in the crystal structure define the stereochemistry at the five previously unassigned stereocenters of GE, as follows: D-dmaDap, D-Ser, D-Val, 3R,4S,L-dhGln, D-aThr, D-iSer, and L-Ama (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3C–E

claim: GE binds within a shallow bowl-like depression formed by the D2 loop, the link region, and the Mg2+ loop, and the H and I regions.
source: GE binds within a shallow bowl-like depression formed by the D2 loop, the link region, and the Mg2+ loop [Mg2+(I) and three RNAP Asp residues that coordinate Mg2+(I)], and the H and I regions (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3C,D

claim: GE is oriented relative to RNAP such that the GE dhGln residue is directed toward Mg2+(I) and the GE dmaDap residue is directed toward the Rif pocket.
source: GE is oriented relative to RNAP such that the GE dhGln residue is directed toward Mg2+(I) and the GE dmaDap residue is directed toward the Rif pocket (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3C–E

claim: The GE dhGln residue participates in a network of interactions, including H-bonds with RNAP βGlu565, βArg678, and βLys1073, an H-bond with a water molecule in the first coordination shell of Mg2+(I), and van der Waals interactions with RNAP β′Asp462.
source: The GE dhGln residue participates in a network of interactions, including H-bonds with RNAP βGlu565, βArg678, and βLys1073, an H-bond with a water molecule in the first coordination shell of Mg2+(I), and van der Waals interactions with RNAP β′Asp462, which is one of the three RNAP Asp residues that coordinate Mg2+(I) (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 3D–E

claim: Modification of the GE dhGln sidechain eliminates RNAP-inhibitory activity.
source: Modification of the GE dhGln sidechain eliminates RNAP-inhibitory activity (Mariani et al., 2005), consistent with the participation by this sidechain in multiple H-bonds and van der Waals interactions with RNAP.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mariani et al., 2005

claim: Removal of the Ama sidechain reduces RNAP-inhibitory activity.
source: Removal of the Ama sidechain reduces RNAP-inhibitory activity (Mariani et al., 2005), consistent with the participation of this sidechain in an H-bond and van der Waals interactions with RNAP.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mariani et al., 2005

claim: Substitutions of the dmaDap sidechain acyl moiety, including substitutions with bulky groups, has little or no effect on RNAP-inhibitory activity.
source: Substitutions of the dmaDap sidechain acyl moiety, including substitutions with bulky groups, has little or no effect on RNAP-inhibitory activity (Mariani et al., 2005), consistent with the fact that atoms of the acyl group are disordered in the structure and are inferred to make few or no interactions with RNAP.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mariani et al., 2005

claim: Promoter DNA binding to form RPo does not change the conformation of GE or the interactions between RNAP and GE.
source: Comparison of the structures of RNAP-GE (Figure 3) and RPo-GE (Figure 4) shows that promoter DNA binding to form RPo does not change the conformation of GE or the interactions between RNAP and GE (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by comparison of crystal structures shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: GE does not change the conformation of DNA or the interactions between RNAP and DNA.
source: Comparison of structures of RPo (Zhang et al., 2012) and RPo-GE (Figure 4) show that GE does not change the conformation of DNA or the interactions between RNAP and DNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by comparison of crystal structures shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: A structural model of a primer-dependent transcription initiation complex predicts severe steric clash between GE and both the RNA 3′ nucleotide in the i site and the NTP in the i+1 site.
source: The resulting structural model predicts severe steric clash between GE and both the RNA 3′ nucleotide in the i site and the NTP in the i+1 site (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The crystal structure of RPo-ATP-CMPcPP provides the first structural information of a substrate complex for de novo transcription by a multi-subunit RNAP.
source: The resulting structure provides the first structural information of a substrate complex for de novo transcription by a multi-subunit RNAP.
evidence: Supported by the novelty of the crystal structure

claim: The base and sugar moieties of the first initiating NTP make the same interactions with DNA and RNAP that the RNA 3′-nucleotide base and sugar make in a transcription elongation complex.
source: The base and sugar moieties of the first initiating NTP make the same interactions with DNA and RNAP that the RNA 3′-nucleotide base and sugar make in a transcription elongation complex (Vassylyev et al., 2007; Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 5C,D and citation to Vassylyev et al., 2007

claim: The triphosphate of the first initiating NTP extends into the space that is occupied by the RNA-1 nucleotide in a transcription elongation complex.
source: The triphosphate of the first initiating NTP extends into the space that is occupied by the RNA-1 nucleotide in a transcription elongation complex, and makes H-bonds and salt-bridges through its γ-phosphate with RNAP βGln688 and βHis1237, and through its α-phosphate with RNAP βLys1065 and βLys1073 (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 5C,D

claim: The sugar and triphosphate of the second initiating NTP make interactions characteristic of a 'preinsertion-mode' elongation complex.
source: The sugar and triphosphate of the second initiating NTP make interactions characteristic of a 'preinsertion-mode' elongation complex, in which the sugar and triphosphate make only a subset of the interactions required for catalysis, and, in particular, in which the triphosphate approaches, but does not coordinate, Mg2+(I) (Vassylyev et al., 2007; Zhang and Landick, 2009; Martinez-Rucobo and Cramer, 2013; Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 5C,D and citations

claim: The 'preinsertion-mode' initiation complex defined herein is an obligatory functional intermediate in formation of the catalytically competent 'insertion-mode' initiation complex.
source: We suggest, by analogy, that the 'preinsertion-mode' initiation complex defined herein is an obligatory functional intermediate in formation of the catalytically competent 'insertion-mode' initiation complex.
evidence: Inferred by analogy to elongation complexes

claim: A structural model by superimposing crystal structures of RPo-GE and RPo-ATP-CMPcPP shows severe steric clash between GE and both the first initiating NTP in the i site and the second initiating NTP in the i+1 site.
source: The resulting structural model shows severe steric clash between GE and both the first initiating NTP in the i site and the second initiating NTP in the i+1 site (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 5E

claim: Electron density maps obtained by soaking a crystal of RPo with ATP and CMPcPP show unambiguous electron density for ATP and CMPcPP in the i and i+1 sites.
source: As described above, electron density maps obtained by soaking a crystal of RPo with ATP and CMPcPP show unambiguous electron density for ATP and CMPcPP in the i and i+1 sites (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Electron density maps obtained by soaking a crystal of RPo first with GE, and then with ATP and CMPcPP show unambiguous electron density for GE, but show no density for ATP or CMPcPP in the i and i+1 sites.
source: In contrast, electron density maps obtained by soaking a crystal of RPo first with GE, and then with ATP and CMPcPP show unambiguous electron density for GE, but show no density for ATP or CMPcPP in the i and i+1 sites (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 5G

claim: GE interferes with binding of initiating NTPs to the i and i+1 sites.
source: We conclude that GE interferes with binding of initiating nucleotides to the RNAP i and i+1 sites.
evidence: Inferred from crystal structure data showing mutually exclusive binding

claim: GE inhibits the binding of Rif to RNAP.
source: The results in Figure 6A–C show that GE inhibits the binding of Rif to RNAP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–C

claim: GE decreases kon for Rif ∼20-fold, increases koff for Rif ∼fourfold, and increases the equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) for Rif ∼80-fold.
source: GE decreases kon for Rif ∼20-fold, increases koff for Rif ∼fourfold, and increases the equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) for Rif ∼80-fold (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: The equilibrium dissociation constant for inhibition of RNAP-Rif interaction by GE (Ki) is 6 nM.
source: The equilibrium dissociation constant for inhibition of RNAP-Rif interaction by GE (Ki) is 6 nM, which is comparable to the IC50 for inhibition of RNAP by GE (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: GE does not preclude the binding of Rif to RNAP.
source: However, the results in Figure 6A–C also show that GE does not preclude the binding of Rif to RNAP.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–C

claim: Even at saturating concentrations of GE, RNAP-Rif interaction still occurs and still exhibits a submicromolar Kd (Kd = 30 nM).
source: Thus, even at saturating concentrations of GE, RNAP-Rif interaction still occurs (Figure 6A) and still exhibits a submicromolar Kd (Kd = 30 nM; Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6C

claim: GE inhibits the binding of Rif to RNAP, but GE and Rif can bind simultaneously to RNAP at sufficient concentrations.
source: We infer that GE inhibits the binding of Rif to RNAP, but that GE and Rif can bind simultaneously to RNAP at sufficient concentrations.
evidence: Inferred from the partial competitive binding data

claim: A structural model predicts that GE bound to the GE target is located immediately adjacent to Rif bound to the Rif target.
source: The structural model predicts that GE bound to the GE target is located immediately adjacent to Rif bound to the Rif target (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 6D

claim: A structural model predicts that there is steric clash between GE bound to the GE target and Rif bound to the Rif target, but that clash is limited to the dmaDap sidechain of GE and the C3 atom and sidechain of Rif.
source: The structural model further predicts that there is steric clash between GE bound to the GE target and Rif bound to the Rif target, but that clash is limited to the dmaDap sidechain of GE and the C3 atom and sidechain of Rif (cyan in Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 6D

claim: The crystal structure of RPo-GE-RifSV shows unambiguous electron density for GE in the GE target and for RifSV in the Rif target.
source: In this case, the resulting electron density maps showed unambiguous electron density for GE in the GE target and for RifSV in the Rif target (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 6H

claim: Occupancy levels for both GE and RifSV were 1, indicating that GE and RifSV were bound simultaneously to RNAP in the crystal.
source: Occupancy levels for both GE and RifSV were 1, indicating that GE and RifSV were bound simultaneously to RNAP in the crystal.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data

claim: The conformation of the GE dmaDap residue differs in RPo-GE and RPo-GE-RifSV.
source: The conformation of the GE dmaDap residue differs in RPo-GE and RPo-GE-RifSV (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: The GE dmaDap sidechain in RPo-GE-RifSV is rotated by ∼110°, in a direction that increases the distance between the dmaDap sidechain carbonyl carbon and the RifSV C3 atom from 3.7 Å to 8.6 Å and thereby alleviates steric clash.
source: The GE dmaDap sidechain in RPo-GE-RifSV is rotated by ∼110°, in a direction that increases the distance between the dmaDap sidechain carbonyl carbon and the RifSV C3 atom from 3.7 Å to 8.6 Å and thereby alleviates steric clash.
evidence: Supported by crystal structure data

claim: A bipartite compound comprising GE, linked through its dmaDap residue, to a rifamycin, linked through its C3 or O4 atom, is possible and tractable to synthesize.
source: Accordingly, synthesis of such a bipartite compound not only is possible, but also is tractable.
evidence: Inferred from the crystal structure and chemical properties of GE and rifamycins

claim: A bipartite compound comprising GE and a rifamycin is expected to have exceptionally high binding affinity, exceptionally high RNAP-inhibitory potency, and an ability to overcome resistance arising from substitutions in one of the GE target and the Rif target.
source: Such a bipartite compound is expected to be able to bind simultaneously to the GE target (through the GE moiety) and the Rif target (through the rifamycin moiety). Accordingly, such a compound is expected to have exceptionally high binding affinity, exceptionally high RNAP-inhibitory potency, and an ability to overcome resistance arising from substitutions in one of the GE target and the Rif target.
evidence: Inferred from the structural and functional properties of GE and rifamycins

claim: A bipartite inhibitor comprising a GE derivative and RifSV (RifaGE-3) inhibits wild-type RNAP with an IC50 at the limit of detection of the assay (IC50 ≤40 nM).
source: The resulting bipartite inhibitor inhibits wild-type RNAP with an IC50 at the limit of detection of the assay (IC50 ≤40 nM), inhibits GER RNAP >2500-fold more potently than GE (Figure 7D), and inhibits RifR RNAP 50-fold more potently than RifSV (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D

claim: RifaGE-3 inhibits GER RNAP >2500-fold more potently than GE.
source: The resulting bipartite inhibitor inhibits wild-type RNAP with an IC50 at the limit of detection of the assay (IC50 ≤40 nM), inhibits GER RNAP >2500-fold more potently than GE (Figure 7D), and inhibits RifR RNAP 50-fold more potently than RifSV (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D

claim: RifaGE-3 inhibits RifR RNAP 50-fold more potently than RifSV.
source: The resulting bipartite inhibitor inhibits wild-type RNAP with an IC50 at the limit of detection of the assay (IC50 ≤40 nM), inhibits GER RNAP >2500-fold more potently than GE (Figure 7D), and inhibits RifR RNAP 50-fold more potently than RifSV (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E

claim: GE inhibits RNAP through a novel mechanism and a novel target.
source: Our results establish GE inhibits RNAP through a novel mechanism and a novel target.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive experimental and structural data

claim: The binding site on RNAP for GE is adjacent to, but does not substantially overlap, the binding site on RNAP for the rifamycin antibacterial drugs.
source: Our results further establish that the binding site on RNAP for GE is adjacent to, but does not substantially overlap, the binding site on RNAP for the rifamycin antibacterial drugs (Figure 2D–F), show that GE and a rifamycin can bind simultaneously to their adjacent binding sites in RNAP (Figure 6), and show that GE and a rifamycin can be covalently linked, through the GE dmaDap sidechain and the rifamycin C3-O4 region, to yield a bipartite RNAP inhibitor that binds to both the GE target and the rifamycin target (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by structural and biochemical data shown in Figures 2D–F, 6, and 7

claim: GE and a rifamycin can bind simultaneously to their adjacent binding sites in RNAP.
source: Our results further establish that the binding site on RNAP for GE is adjacent to, but does not substantially overlap, the binding site on RNAP for the rifamycin antibacterial drugs (Figure 2D–F), show that GE and a rifamycin can bind simultaneously to their adjacent binding sites in RNAP (Figure 6), and show that GE and a rifamycin can be covalently linked, through the GE dmaDap sidechain and the rifamycin C3-O4 region, to yield a bipartite RNAP inhibitor that binds to both the GE target and the rifamycin target (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by structural and biochemical data shown in Figure 6

claim: GE and a rifamycin can be covalently linked, through the GE dmaDap sidechain and the rifamycin C3-O4 region, to yield a bipartite RNAP inhibitor that binds to both the GE target and the rifamycin target.
source: Our results further establish that the binding site on RNAP for GE is adjacent to, but does not substantially overlap, the binding site on RNAP for the rifamycin antibacterial drugs (Figure 2D–F), show that GE and a rifamycin can bind simultaneously to their adjacent binding sites in RNAP (Figure 6), and show that GE and a rifamycin can be covalently linked, through the GE dmaDap sidechain and the rifamycin C3-O4 region, to yield a bipartite RNAP inhibitor that binds to both the GE target and the rifamycin target (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by structural and biochemical data shown in Figure 7

claim: The GE target is an unusually attractive target—a 'privileged target'—for antibacterial drug discovery involving RNAP.
source: Three features of the GE target, identified in this work, indicate that the GE target is an unusually attractive target—a 'privileged target'—for antibacterial drug discovery involving RNAP.
evidence: Inferred from the three features described in the text

claim: Most residues of the GE binding site are functionally critical residues of the RNAP active center that cannot be substituted without loss of RNAP activity.
source: First, since most residues of the GE binding site are functionally critical residues of the RNAP active center that cannot be substituted without loss of RNAP activity, the target-based resistance spectra of an antibacterial compound that functions through the GE binding site will be small (∼1/10 the size of the target-based resistance spectrum of Rif; ∼1/10 to ∼1/5 the size of the target-based resistance spectra of RNAP inhibitors; Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from structural and genetic data

claim: The GE binding site is different from the rifamycin binding site.
source: Second, since the GE binding site is different from the rifamycin binding site, an antibacterial compound that functions through the GE binding site will not exhibit target-based cross-resistance with rifamycins (Figure 2E,F; Supplementary file 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by structural and genetic data shown in Figure 2E,F and Supplementary files 2D,E

claim: An antibacterial compound that functions through the GE binding site will not exhibit target-based cross-resistance with rifamycins.
source: Second, since the GE binding site is different from the rifamycin binding site, an antibacterial compound that functions through the GE binding site will not exhibit target-based cross-resistance with rifamycins (Figure 2E,F; Supplementary file 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,F and Supplementary files 2D,E

claim: An antibacterial compound that functions through the GE binding site can be linked to a rifamycin or a sorangicin to construct a bipartite, bivalent inhibitor that binds to both the GE target and the rifamycin target and, therefore, that is exceptionally potent and exceptionally refractory to target-based resistance.
source: Third, since the GE binding site is adjacent to, but does not substantially overlap, the rifamycin binding site (Figures 2D and 6), an antibacterial compound that functions through the GE binding site can be linked to a rifamycin or a sorangicin to construct a bipartite, bivalent inhibitor that binds to both the GE target and the rifamycin target and, therefore, that is exceptionally potent and exceptionally refractory to target-based resistance (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by structural and biochemical data shown in Figures 2D, 6, and 7
